title: Bacteria, Viruses & Microbial Growth
description: Prokaryotic structure, Gram and acid-fast staining, growth curves and requirements, microbial metabolism and genetics, viruses and their replication, fungi and protists, sterilization, antibiotics and resistance.

cards.title: Name the three basic shapes of bacterial cells and the Latin-derived term for each.
cards.body:
**Cocci** (spheres), **bacilli** (rods) and **spirals**.

Spirals include the rigid spirilla, the flexible spirochetes, and comma-shaped vibrios.

Example: $\textit{Staphylococcus aureus}$ is a coccus, $\textit{Escherichia coli}$ is a bacillus, $\textit{Vibrio cholerae}$ is a curved rod.
Tip: shape and arrangement are the first clues when you look at a Gram-stained smear.
cards.searchQuery: bacterial cell shapes cocci bacilli spirals

cards.title: How do $\textit{Staphylococcus}$ and $\textit{Streptococcus}$ cells arrange themselves, and why do they differ?
cards.body:
**Staphylococci** form grape-like clusters; **streptococci** form chains.

Cocci divide by binary fission and stay attached. Staphylococci divide in several random planes, giving clusters. Streptococci divide in one plane only, giving chains.

Mnemonic: STREP = a STRing of beads; STAPH = a STack of grapes.
cards.searchQuery: staphylococcus clusters streptococcus chains division planes

cards.title: What is the usual method of asexual reproduction in bacteria, in which one cell elongates and splits into two identical cells?
cards.body:
Binary fission.

The chromosome replicates, the cell elongates, and a septum forms between the two copies. Each daughter cell is a genetic clone barring mutation.

Key idea: one cell becomes two, so the population doubles each generation.
cards.searchQuery: bacteria binary fission reproduction steps

cards.title: Which anionic polymers of glycerol or ribitol phosphate occur only in Gram-positive walls, anchored to peptidoglycan or to the plasma membrane?
cards.body:
Teichoic acids.

They add negative charge to the Gram-positive wall and help bind ions. **Lipoteichoic acids** attach to the plasma membrane; **wall teichoic acids** attach to peptidoglycan.

Watch out: Gram-negative bacteria have no teichoic acids; they have an outer membrane instead.
cards.searchQuery: teichoic acids Gram-positive cell wall lipoteichoic

cards.title: Which component of the lipopolysaccharide (LPS) in the Gram-negative outer membrane acts as the endotoxin that can cause fever and septic shock?
cards.body:
Lipid A.

When Gram-negative cells die and lyse, lipid A is released and activates macrophages through TLR4, causing release of cytokines. The result is fever, and in excess, septic shock.

Key idea: **endotoxin** is LPS (its lipid A part), while exotoxins are secreted proteins.
cards.searchQuery: lipid A endotoxin LPS Gram-negative septic shock

cards.title: What are the protein channels in the Gram-negative outer membrane that let small hydrophilic molecules diffuse into the cell?
cards.body:
Porins.

These beta-barrel proteins let small hydrophilic molecules such as nutrients and some antibiotics cross the outer membrane. The outer membrane otherwise blocks large molecules and hydrophobic compounds.

Why: this is part of why Gram-negative bacteria resist many drugs that Gram-positives do not.
cards.searchQuery: porins Gram-negative outer membrane channels

cards.title: Where is the periplasmic space in a Gram-negative cell, and what does it contain?
cards.body:
Between the **plasma membrane** and the **outer membrane**.

It holds the thin peptidoglycan layer, nutrient-binding and transport proteins, and degradative enzymes such as $\beta$-lactamases.

Why: this compartment is one reason Gram-negative bacteria can inactivate some antibiotics before they reach their targets.
cards.searchQuery: periplasmic space Gram-negative contents peptidoglycan

cards.title: Which two Gram-positive genera are the medically important endospore-formers?
cards.body:
$\textit{Bacillus}$ and $\textit{Clostridium}$.

Examples: $\textit{Bacillus anthracis}$ (anthrax), $\textit{Clostridium tetani}$ (tetanus), $\textit{Clostridium botulinum}$ (botulism).

Watch out: spores are for **survival**, not reproduction. One vegetative cell makes one endospore, which germinates into one cell.
cards.searchQuery: endospore forming bacteria Bacillus Clostridium

cards.title: Which calcium-chelated compound, abundant in the endospore core, helps protect it from heat and drying?
cards.body:
Dipicolinic acid.

Calcium dipicolinate together with small acid-soluble proteins stabilizes DNA, and the core is highly dehydrated. This makes spores survive boiling, which is why autoclaving is needed to sterilize.
cards.searchQuery: dipicolinic acid endospore core heat resistance

cards.title: List the four steps of the Gram stain in order.
cards.body:
1. **Crystal violet** (primary stain)
2. **Gram's iodine** (mordant)
3. **Alcohol or acetone** (decolorizer)
4. **Safranin** (counterstain)

Gram-positive cells keep the violet complex; Gram-negative cells lose it and take up pink safranin.

Mnemonic: Violet, Iodine, Decolorize, Safranin = "Very Intelligent Dogs Sit".
cards.searchQuery: Gram stain procedure steps crystal violet iodine safranin

cards.title: In the Gram stain, iodine forms a large crystal violet-iodine complex inside the cell. What type of reagent is iodine?
cards.body:
A mordant.

Iodine binds crystal violet to form a large complex that is hard to wash out of thick peptidoglycan. A mordant fixes a dye so it resists removal.

Watch out: iodine is not the decolorizer. That is alcohol or acetone.
cards.searchQuery: Gram stain iodine mordant crystal violet complex

cards.title: What happens to Gram-positive cells that are over-decolorized during the Gram stain?
cards.body:
They lose the crystal violet and appear **pink**, falsely reading as Gram-negative.

The decolorizer dehydrates the thick peptidoglycan and shrinks its pores, trapping the violet complex. Too much alcohol overcomes this.

Watch out: very old Gram-positive cultures also stain Gram-variable because their walls break down.
cards.searchQuery: Gram stain over-decolorizing Gram-positive appear pink

cards.title: Which waxy, long-chain fatty acid in the wall of $\textit{Mycobacterium}$ makes it acid-fast?
cards.body:
Mycolic acid.

This lipid makes the wall hydrophobic, so mycobacteria resist the Gram stain, stain slowly, and then hold dye even against acid-alcohol. It also makes them resistant to drying and many disinfectants.
cards.searchQuery: mycolic acid Mycobacterium acid-fast wall

cards.title: In the Ziehl-Neelsen acid-fast stain, what color are acid-fast bacteria and what color are non-acid-fast cells?
cards.body:
Acid-fast cells are **red** (carbol fuchsin); non-acid-fast cells are **blue** (methylene blue counterstain).

Steps: carbol fuchsin with heat, then acid-alcohol decolorizer, then methylene blue.

Example: red rods in sputum suggest $\textit{Mycobacterium tuberculosis}$.
cards.searchQuery: Ziehl-Neelsen acid-fast stain colors carbol fuchsin

cards.title: In the Schaeffer-Fulton endospore stain, what color are the endospores and what color are the vegetative cells?
cards.body:
Endospores are **green** (malachite green, applied with heat); vegetative cells are **pink to red** (safranin counterstain).

Heat is needed to drive the dye through the tough spore coat. Once inside, the dye is retained even after the water rinse.
cards.searchQuery: Schaeffer-Fulton endospore stain malachite green safranin

cards.title: Why are $\textit{Mycoplasma}$ species resistant to penicillin and invisible to the Gram stain?
cards.body:
They have **no cell wall**.

Penicillin blocks peptidoglycan cross-linking, so it has no target. Their plasma membrane contains sterols, which helps stabilize it without a wall.

Example: $\textit{Mycoplasma pneumoniae}$ causes atypical (walking) pneumonia and is treated with macrolides or tetracyclines instead.
cards.searchQuery: Mycoplasma no cell wall penicillin resistant sterols

cards.title: Archaea and bacteria are both prokaryotes. Which of them resembles eukaryotes more in its RNA polymerase and histone-like DNA proteins?
cards.body:
Archaea.

They lack peptidoglycan and have ether-linked membrane lipids, yet their transcription and translation machinery resembles the eukaryotic versions. Many species live in extreme habitats such as hot springs or high salt.

Key idea: archaea are prokaryotic in structure but share genetic machinery with eukaryotes.
cards.searchQuery: archaea similar to eukaryotes RNA polymerase histones

cards.title: What flagella-like structures lie inside the periplasm of spirochetes such as $\textit{Treponema pallidum}$ and drive their corkscrew motion?
cards.body:
Axial filaments.

They are anchored at the cell poles and wrap around the cell inside the outer sheath. Rotation twists the whole cell like a corkscrew, which lets spirochetes bore through viscous tissue.

Example: this motion helps $\textit{Treponema pallidum}$ (syphilis) and $\textit{Borrelia burgdorferi}$ (Lyme disease) invade tissues.
cards.searchQuery: axial filaments spirochete endoflagella motility

cards.title: Which short, numerous hairlike surface appendages let bacteria attach to host tissues, as in $\textit{Neisseria gonorrhoeae}$?
cards.body:
Fimbriae.

They are distinct from the longer, rarer sex pilus used in conjugation. Loss of fimbriae often makes a pathogen unable to colonize.
cards.searchQuery: fimbriae bacterial adhesion attachment Neisseria gonorrhoeae

cards.title: Name the four phases of a bacterial growth curve in a closed (batch) culture, in order.
cards.body:
**Lag**, **log (exponential)**, **stationary** and **death (decline)**.

On a plot of $\log_{10}$ viable cells against time, the log phase is a straight line because the population doubles at a constant rate.

Watch out: the y-axis is usually logarithmic. On a linear axis, the log phase looks like an upward curve.
cards.searchQuery: bacterial growth curve phases lag log stationary death

cards.title: Which growth phase follows inoculation into fresh medium, when cells adapt and make enzymes and metabolites but show little or no division?
cards.body:
The lag phase.

Cells are metabolically active, not dormant. They synthesize the ribosomes, enzymes and cofactors needed for the new medium. Lag is longer if the inoculum was old or the medium is very different.
cards.searchQuery: lag phase bacterial growth adaptation no division

cards.title: In which growth phase do cells divide at a constant, maximal rate, and are most vulnerable to antibiotics such as penicillin?
cards.body:
The log (exponential) phase.

Penicillin kills only cells that are actively building new cell wall, so growing cells are the most susceptible. Cells in this phase are also the most uniform in size and physiology.
cards.searchQuery: log exponential phase bacteria antibiotic susceptibility

cards.title: Why does a batch culture level off into the stationary phase?
cards.body:
Nutrients run low and toxic wastes build up, so the **rate of cell division equals the rate of cell death**.

The viable count stays roughly constant. Cells often make secondary metabolites, and spore-formers begin sporulation.

Key idea: a plateau means a balance of division and death, not that all growth has stopped.
cards.searchQuery: stationary phase bacterial growth nutrient depletion waste

cards.title: About how many minutes is the generation time of $\textit{E. coli}$ in rich medium at $37\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$? Give the number only.
cards.body:
About 20 minutes.

Generation time is the time it takes a population to double. It varies hugely among species: $\textit{E. coli}$ is around 20 min under ideal conditions, while $\textit{Mycobacterium tuberculosis}$ is roughly 15 to 20 hours.

Why: slow growth is why TB cultures take weeks and why TB treatment lasts months.
cards.searchQuery: E. coli generation time 20 minutes doubling

cards.title: Write the equation for the number of cells $N_t$ after $n$ generations, starting from $N_0$ cells, and how $n$ is found from time $t$ and generation time $g$.
cards.body:
$N_t = N_0 \times 2^n$, with $n = t/g$.

Each generation doubles the population. To find $n$ from cell counts, use $n = \log_2(N_t/N_0) = \dfrac{\log_{10}(N_t/N_0)}{0.301}$.

Example: 1 cell with $g = 20$ min gives $2^{6} = 64$ cells after 2 h.
Watch out: $t$ and $g$ must be in the same units.
cards.searchQuery: bacterial growth equation Nt N0 2^n generations

cards.title: A culture starts with 100 cells and has a generation time of 30 min. How many cells are present after 3 h of exponential growth? Give the number only.
cards.body:
6400

Number of generations: $n = 180/30 = 6$.

$N = 100 \times 2^6 = 100 \times 64 = 6400$.

Tip: do the generations first, then the power of 2.
cards.searchQuery: calculate bacterial cells after generations doubling problem

cards.title: A culture grows exponentially from $10^3$ to $10^6$ cells in 2.0 h. What is its generation time in minutes, rounded to the nearest minute? Give the number only.
cards.body:
12

Generations: $n = \log_2(10^6/10^3) = \log_2(1000) = 3/0.301 \approx 9.97$.

Generation time: $g = 120\,\mathrm{min}/9.97 \approx 12.0\,\mathrm{min}$.

Watch out: use $\log_2$ (or divide the base-10 log by 0.301), not the base-10 log alone.
cards.searchQuery: calculate bacterial generation time from cell counts

cards.title: Which temperature class of microbe, with optima of roughly $20$ to $45\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, includes most human pathogens?
cards.body:
Mesophiles.

Human body temperature (about $37\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$) falls right in their range. The other classes are psychrophiles (cold), thermophiles (hot) and hyperthermophiles (above about $80\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, mostly archaea).
cards.searchQuery: mesophiles temperature range human pathogens

cards.title: Which Gram-positive foodborne pathogen can multiply at refrigerator temperature ($4\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$) in deli meats and soft cheeses?
cards.body:
$\textit{Listeria monocytogenes}$.

It is a psychrotroph: it grows best at moderate temperatures but still grows in the cold. Infection is most dangerous in pregnancy, newborns and immunocompromised people.

Watch out: refrigeration slows most bacteria but does not stop all of them.
cards.searchQuery: Listeria monocytogenes grows refrigerator temperature psychrotroph

cards.title: In a fluid thioglycolate tube, growth appears only at the very top where oxygen is highest. Which oxygen-requirement class is this?
cards.body:
Obligate aerobe.

These organisms need $\ce{O2}$ as the final electron acceptor for aerobic respiration.

Example: $\textit{Mycobacterium tuberculosis}$ and $\textit{Pseudomonas aeruginosa}$.
cards.searchQuery: thioglycolate broth obligate aerobe growth at top

cards.title: In a thioglycolate tube, growth is only at the bottom. Which oxygen-requirement class is this, and why does oxygen harm these cells?
cards.body:
**Obligate anaerobe.**

They lack, or have little, superoxide dismutase and catalase, so toxic oxygen products such as superoxide and hydrogen peroxide accumulate.

Example: $\textit{Clostridium}$ and $\textit{Bacteroides}$ species.
cards.searchQuery: obligate anaerobe thioglycolate growth at bottom superoxide dismutase

cards.title: In a thioglycolate tube, growth occurs throughout, but is densest at the top. Which oxygen-requirement class is this?
cards.body:
Facultative anaerobe.

They use aerobic respiration when oxygen is available, because it yields more ATP, and switch to fermentation or anaerobic respiration when it is not.

Example: $\textit{Escherichia coli}$ and $\textit{Staphylococcus aureus}$.
cards.searchQuery: facultative anaerobe thioglycolate growth pattern E. coli

cards.title: In a thioglycolate tube, growth is evenly spread from top to bottom. These cells ferment but tolerate oxygen. Which class is this?
cards.body:
Aerotolerant anaerobe.

They cannot use oxygen to make ATP, but they have enough protection (such as superoxide dismutase) to survive it. Even growth shows that oxygen neither helps nor harms.

Example: many $\textit{Streptococcus}$ species.
cards.searchQuery: aerotolerant anaerobe thioglycolate even growth Streptococcus

cards.title: What is a microaerophile, and which two pathogens are examples?
cards.body:
A microaerophile needs **low oxygen** (about 2 to 10%) and is harmed by the full atmospheric level (about 21%).

Examples: $\textit{Campylobacter jejuni}$ and $\textit{Helicobacter pylori}$.

Why: in a thioglycolate tube they form a band a little below the surface, where oxygen is low but not zero.
cards.searchQuery: microaerophile low oxygen Campylobacter Helicobacter

cards.title: Which two enzymes let aerobes and aerotolerant cells detoxify superoxide and hydrogen peroxide, and what does each do?
cards.body:
**Superoxide dismutase (SOD)** converts $\ce{O2^-}$ to $\ce{H2O2}$ and $\ce{O2}$. **Catalase** converts $\ce{H2O2}$ to $\ce{H2O}$ and $\ce{O2}$.

Example: bubbling when a drop of $\ce{H2O2}$ meets a colony is the catalase test.
Tip: catalase-negative streptococci vs catalase-positive staphylococci is a classic first split.
cards.searchQuery: superoxide dismutase catalase oxygen toxicity bacteria

cards.title: What term describes microbes that grow best at an acidic pH, below about 5.5? Most pathogens, by contrast, prefer near-neutral pH.
cards.body:
Acidophiles.

Most human pathogens are **neutrophils**, preferring about pH 6.5 to 7.5. Fungi often tolerate acid better than bacteria, which is why acidic foods spoil more often by molds.

Example: $\textit{Helicobacter pylori}$ survives stomach acid by making urease.
cards.searchQuery: acidophiles pH preference neutrophiles alkaliphiles

cards.title: How does a selective medium differ from a differential medium?
cards.body:
A **selective** medium allows some organisms to grow and inhibits others. A **differential** medium lets all grow but makes them look different.

Many media do both.

Example: MacConkey agar contains bile salts and crystal violet, which select for Gram-negative rods, and lactose with a pH indicator, which separates lactose fermenters (pink) from non-fermenters (colorless).
cards.searchQuery: selective versus differential media MacConkey agar

cards.title: By energy source and carbon source, what nutritional type are most human pathogens?
cards.body:
Chemoheterotrophs.

They get energy from chemical compounds (chemo-) and carbon from organic molecules (hetero-), in this case from the host.

Key idea: the other types are photoautotrophs (light and $\ce{CO2}$, as in cyanobacteria), chemoautotrophs (inorganic chemicals and $\ce{CO2}$) and photoheterotrophs.
cards.searchQuery: chemoheterotroph nutritional types phototroph chemotroph

cards.title: Which glucose-breakdown pathway, used by $\textit{Pseudomonas}$ in place of glycolysis, nets only $1$ ATP per glucose?
cards.body:
The Entner–Doudoroff pathway

Glucose 6-phosphate is oxidized to 6-phosphogluconate, which is split into pyruvate and glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate. Per glucose, the net yield is $1$ ATP, $1$ NADH and $1$ NADPH.

Example: $\textit{Pseudomonas}$ and $\textit{Zymomonas}$ use it as their main route for glucose.
Watch out: glycolysis (the Embden–Meyerhof pathway) nets $2$ ATP per glucose.
cards.searchQuery: Entner-Doudoroff pathway bacteria net ATP per glucose

cards.title: Fermentation yields no extra ATP beyond glycolysis. What is its essential purpose for the cell?
cards.body:
It **regenerates $\ce{NAD+}$** from NADH, so glycolysis can keep running.

Pyruvate or a derivative is reduced by NADH, and the end products (lactic acid, ethanol, and others) are excreted. Without oxygen or another external electron acceptor, there is no other way to recycle $\ce{NAD+}$.

Watch out: fermentation does not use an electron transport chain.
cards.searchQuery: fermentation purpose regenerate NAD+ glycolysis

cards.title: Which genus of Gram-positive rods ferments lactose to lactic acid in yogurt and is part of the normal vaginal flora?
cards.body:
$\textit{Lactobacillus}$.

The lactic acid it makes lowers the pH, which preserves dairy foods and protects the vagina by discouraging other microbes.
cards.searchQuery: Lactobacillus lactic acid fermentation yogurt vaginal flora

cards.title: Write the overall equation for alcoholic fermentation of glucose by yeast, and name the yeast.
cards.body:
$\ce{C6H12O6 -> 2 C2H5OH + 2 CO2}$, by $\textit{Saccharomyces cerevisiae}$.

Pyruvate is first decarboxylated to acetaldehyde, which NADH then reduces to ethanol. The $\ce{CO2}$ makes bread rise and beer fizzy.

Example: net yield is still only 2 ATP per glucose, from glycolysis.
cards.searchQuery: alcoholic fermentation yeast ethanol CO2 equation

cards.title: How does anaerobic respiration differ from fermentation?
cards.body:
Anaerobic respiration uses an **electron transport chain** with a final electron acceptor other than $\ce{O2}$. Fermentation uses no electron transport chain.

Common acceptors are nitrate ($\ce{NO3-}$), sulfate ($\ce{SO4^2-}$) and carbonate. Yield is usually lower than aerobic respiration because these acceptors have lower reduction potentials.

Example: $\textit{Pseudomonas}$ species can use nitrate; $\textit{Desulfovibrio}$ reduces sulfate to $\ce{H2S}$.
cards.searchQuery: anaerobic respiration versus fermentation terminal electron acceptor

cards.title: Where is the electron transport chain located in a bacterial cell, since bacteria have no mitochondria?
cards.body:
The plasma membrane.

Protons are pumped across it to the periplasm or outside, and the proton motive force then drives ATP synthase, just as in the inner mitochondrial membrane.

Key idea: this supports the endosymbiotic origin of mitochondria.
cards.searchQuery: bacterial electron transport chain plasma membrane proton motive force

cards.title: Which enzyme, found in $\textit{Rhizobium}$ in legume root nodules, reduces atmospheric $\ce{N2}$ to ammonia?
cards.body:
Nitrogenase.

This process is **nitrogen fixation**: $\ce{N2 -> NH3}$, which plants can use. The enzyme is destroyed by oxygen, so nodules keep oxygen low with leghemoglobin.

Example: free-living fixers include $\textit{Azotobacter}$ and cyanobacteria.
cards.searchQuery: nitrogenase nitrogen fixation Rhizobium root nodules

cards.title: Which species of $\textit{Staphylococcus}$ is coagulase-positive, unlike most other staphylococci such as $\textit{S. epidermidis}$?
cards.body:
$\textit{Staphylococcus aureus}$.

Coagulase converts fibrinogen to fibrin, clotting plasma. It is used clinically to separate the more virulent $\textit{S. aureus}$ from coagulase-negative staphylococci.

Tip: Gram-positive cocci in clusters, catalase-positive, coagulase-positive = $\textit{S. aureus}$.
cards.searchQuery: coagulase test Staphylococcus aureus positive

cards.title: What are the three mechanisms of horizontal gene transfer in bacteria?
cards.body:
**Transformation** (uptake of naked DNA), **transduction** (DNA carried by a bacteriophage) and **conjugation** (DNA transferred through cell-to-cell contact).

Horizontal transfer moves genes between cells of the same generation, not parent to offspring. It spreads antibiotic resistance and virulence genes.

Mnemonic: Transformation = naked DNA; Transduction = phage; Conjugation = contact.
cards.searchQuery: horizontal gene transfer transformation transduction conjugation

cards.title: In Griffith's 1928 experiment with $\textit{Streptococcus pneumoniae}$, what killed the mice, and what did the result reveal?
cards.body:
Mice died after injection of **live rough (R) cells mixed with heat-killed smooth (S) cells**.

Alive R cells acquired the S trait, a capsule, from dead S cells. This is **transformation**. In 1944, Avery, MacLeod and McCarty showed the transforming principle was DNA.

Watch out: neither heat-killed S cells alone nor live R cells alone killed the mice.
cards.searchQuery: Griffith experiment transformation Streptococcus pneumoniae Avery

cards.title: Which horizontal gene transfer mechanism uses a bacteriophage to carry bacterial DNA from a donor cell to a recipient?
cards.body:
Transduction.

A phage particle accidentally packages bacterial DNA instead of (or along with) its own genome and injects it into the next host.
cards.searchQuery: transduction bacteriophage horizontal gene transfer

cards.title: What is an Hfr cell, and why does conjugation with it rarely turn the recipient into an F-positive cell?
cards.body:
An Hfr (high-frequency recombination) cell has the **F plasmid integrated into its chromosome**.

Conjugation transfers a strand of chromosomal DNA starting at the integrated origin. The whole chromosome takes about 100 min to transfer, so the connection usually breaks first and the recipient does not receive the entire F factor.

Key idea: F+ cells transfer the plasmid; Hfr cells transfer chromosomal genes.
cards.searchQuery: Hfr cell F plasmid integrated chromosome conjugation transfer

cards.title: How do generalized and specialized transduction differ?
cards.body:
**Generalized**: a lytic phage mistakenly packages a random piece of host DNA. **Specialized**: a lysogenic phage excises imprecisely and carries only the host genes next to its integration site.

Example: phage $\lambda$ integrated near the $\textit{gal}$ and $\textit{bio}$ genes of $\textit{E. coli}$ can carry them in specialized transduction.
cards.searchQuery: generalized versus specialized transduction lambda phage

cards.title: What is lysogenic conversion, and which toxins of $\textit{Corynebacterium diphtheriae}$ and $\textit{Vibrio cholerae}$ are examples?
cards.body:
A prophage in the bacterial chromosome gives the host a **new trait**, often a toxin.

Examples: the diphtheria toxin gene is carried by a prophage in $\textit{C. diphtheriae}$, and cholera toxin is encoded by a phage in $\textit{V. cholerae}$. Shiga toxin of $\textit{E. coli}$ O157:H7 is also phage-encoded.

Key idea: nontoxic strains become pathogens by acquiring phage DNA.
cards.searchQuery: lysogenic conversion prophage toxin diphtheria cholera

cards.title: In the $\textit{lac}$ operon, when are the structural genes transcribed at a high rate?
cards.body:
When **lactose is present and glucose is absent**.

Allolactose binds the repressor, which releases the operator (induction). Low glucose raises cAMP, and the cAMP-CAP complex helps RNA polymerase bind the promoter.

Watch out: lactose present with glucose also present gives only low transcription, because there is no CAP activation.
cards.searchQuery: lac operon allolactose repressor CAP cAMP glucose

cards.title: How is the $\textit{trp}$ operon regulated, and what is tryptophan's role?
cards.body:
It is a **repressible** operon. Tryptophan acts as a **corepressor**.

When tryptophan is plentiful, it binds the repressor and the active complex blocks the operator, so the biosynthetic genes are switched off.

Key idea: inducible operons (like $\textit{lac}$) catabolize; repressible operons (like $\textit{trp}$) are usually anabolic.
cards.searchQuery: trp operon repressible corepressor tryptophan

cards.title: In bacteria, what name is given to a cluster of genes under a single promoter that is transcribed into one mRNA?
cards.body:
An operon.

The resulting mRNA, a **polycistronic** message, encodes several proteins, each with its own ribosome-binding site.

Why: bacteria have no nucleus, so ribosomes can begin translating while transcription is still in progress.
cards.searchQuery: operon polycistronic mRNA bacteria single promoter

cards.title: What is the simplest bacterial transposable element, carrying only a transposase gene flanked by inverted repeats?
cards.body:
An insertion sequence (IS element)

IS elements are short (usually under about $2.5$ kb) and move using the **transposase** they encode. Two IS elements flanking other genes form a **composite transposon**, which can carry antibiotic resistance genes.

Why: transposons can jump onto plasmids, which then spread resistance between bacteria by conjugation.
cards.searchQuery: insertion sequence IS element transposase inverted repeats bacteria

cards.title: What enzymes cut DNA at specific palindromic sequences and protect bacteria from invading phage DNA?
cards.body:
Restriction endonucleases.

The host's own DNA is protected because it is methylated at the same sites. Unmethylated phage DNA is cut.

Example: $\textit{Eco}$RI cuts $\mathrm{G\!\downarrow\!AATTC}$ and leaves sticky ends, which is why it is widely used in cloning.
cards.searchQuery: restriction endonucleases palindrome phage defense methylation

cards.title: What does the Ames test detect, and how does it work?
cards.body:
It detects **mutagens**, many of which are carcinogens.

Histidine-requiring $\textit{Salmonella}$ mutants are plated without histidine with the test chemical. Mutagens cause reversions to $\textit{his}^+$, so more colonies grow than on the control plate.

Why: a liver extract (S9) is added because some chemicals become mutagenic only after metabolism.
cards.searchQuery: Ames test mutagen Salmonella histidine reversion

cards.title: What is the natural function of CRISPR-Cas systems in bacteria and archaea?
cards.body:
An **adaptive defense against phages and plasmids**.

Fragments of invader DNA are stored as spacers in the CRISPR array. Their RNA copies guide Cas nucleases to cut matching DNA if the invader returns.

Example: Cas9 guided by a designed RNA is used as a gene-editing tool.
cards.searchQuery: CRISPR Cas bacterial adaptive immunity phage spacers

cards.title: Viruses have no ribosomes and no metabolism of their own. What phrase describes this absolute dependence on a host cell to replicate?
cards.body:
Obligate intracellular parasites.

A virus can only reproduce by taking over the host's ribosomes, nucleotides, amino acids and energy supply. Outside a cell, a virion is inert.

Watch out: viruses are not made of cells and are not treated with antibiotics.
cards.searchQuery: viruses obligate intracellular parasites host cell replication

cards.title: What are the basic components of a virion, and what is the protein shell called?
cards.body:
A **nucleic acid genome** (DNA or RNA, never both) surrounded by a protein shell called the **capsid**.

The capsid is built of subunits called capsomeres. Some viruses also have a lipid envelope with spike glycoproteins.

Key idea: capsid plus genome is the nucleocapsid.
cards.searchQuery: virion structure capsid capsomeres genome envelope

cards.title: Where does a viral envelope come from, and how does having one affect a virus's resistance to soap, alcohol and drying?
cards.body:
The envelope is taken from the **host membrane** as the virus buds out. Enveloped viruses are **fragile**; naked (nonenveloped) viruses are hardy.

Soap and alcohol disrupt lipid envelopes, so enveloped viruses such as influenza are inactivated easily. Naked viruses such as norovirus resist drying, alcohol and bile.

Why: this is why norovirus spreads on surfaces and hand-washing with soap and water matters.
cards.searchQuery: enveloped versus nonenveloped viruses resistance disinfectants

cards.title: List the five stages of the lytic cycle of a bacteriophage in order.
cards.body:
1. **Attachment** to a specific receptor
2. **Penetration** (the phage injects its genome)
3. **Biosynthesis** of phage nucleic acids and proteins
4. **Maturation** (assembly of virions)
5. **Release** by lysis of the cell

The host DNA is degraded and the cell is converted into a phage factory.

Key idea: the lytic cycle kills the host, since the cell bursts.
cards.searchQuery: bacteriophage lytic cycle steps attachment penetration lysis

cards.title: What happens in the lysogenic cycle, and what can trigger it to switch to the lytic cycle?
cards.body:
The phage genome **integrates into the host chromosome** as a prophage and is copied with it at each cell division, with no virions made.

Induction by stress such as UV light or DNA damage excises the prophage and starts the lytic cycle.

Key idea: the host cell survives and passes the phage DNA to its daughters.
cards.searchQuery: lysogenic cycle prophage integration induction UV

cards.title: What term describes a bacteriophage, such as phage $\lambda$, that can enter either the lytic or the lysogenic cycle?
cards.body:
A temperate phage.

A **virulent** phage can only be lytic and always kills the host. A temperate phage can choose between lysis and lysogeny, depending on conditions.
cards.searchQuery: temperate phage versus virulent phage lysogeny

cards.title: What is the integrated DNA copy of a retrovirus such as HIV in the host genome called?
cards.body:
A provirus.

It is made by reverse transcription and integrated by the viral integrase. The provirus is then copied with the host DNA and can stay silent for years.

Watch out: the term for the bacterial analog is "prophage".
cards.searchQuery: provirus integrated retrovirus DNA HIV integrase

cards.title: Which viral enzyme makes DNA from an RNA template, and which family of viruses carries it in the virion?
cards.body:
**Reverse transcriptase**, carried by **retroviruses** such as HIV.

It makes a DNA copy of the RNA genome, which integrase inserts into the host genome. Reverse transcriptase lacks proofreading, so HIV mutates rapidly.

Example: zidovudine (AZT) is a nucleoside analog that blocks reverse transcriptase.
cards.searchQuery: reverse transcriptase retrovirus HIV RNA to DNA

cards.title: Which cell surface proteins does HIV gp120 bind to enter a cell, and which cell type is the main target?
cards.body:
gp120 binds **CD4** and then a coreceptor, **CCR5** or **CXCR4**.

The main targets are CD4$^+$ helper T cells, and also macrophages and dendritic cells. Loss of helper T cells leads to AIDS.

Key idea: a CD4 count below 200 cells per $\mu$L defines AIDS.
cards.searchQuery: HIV gp120 CD4 CCR5 CXCR4 helper T cells

cards.title: How do positive-sense and negative-sense single-stranded RNA viruses differ in how they start infection?
cards.body:
A **positive-sense** genome acts directly as mRNA and is translated at once. A **negative-sense** genome must first be copied into mRNA by an **RNA-dependent RNA polymerase** carried in the virion.

Example: poliovirus and SARS-CoV-2 are positive-sense; influenza virus and measles virus are negative-sense.

Watch out: naked positive-sense RNA is infectious by itself, but naked negative-sense RNA is not.
cards.searchQuery: positive sense versus negative sense RNA virus replication

cards.title: How do antigenic drift and antigenic shift differ in influenza A viruses?
cards.body:
**Drift** is the gradual accumulation of point mutations in the HA and NA genes. **Shift** is a sudden major change from **reassortment** of genome segments between different strains.

Drift explains why seasonal vaccines must be updated yearly. Shift can produce a new subtype that causes a pandemic.

Example: a pig infected with human and avian viruses can be a mixing vessel for reassortment.
cards.searchQuery: influenza antigenic drift versus antigenic shift reassortment

cards.title: How many negative-sense RNA segments make up the genome of influenza A virus? Give the number only.
cards.body:
8

The segmented genome is what allows **reassortment** when two strains infect one cell, which is the molecular basis of antigenic shift.

Watch out: only influenza A and B have 8 segments; influenza C has 7.
cards.searchQuery: influenza A genome 8 RNA segments reassortment

cards.title: What are the roles of hemagglutinin (H) and neuraminidase (N) in influenza, and which drug class targets one of them?
cards.body:
**H** binds sialic acid receptors to attach to and enter the cell. **N** cleaves sialic acid so new virions can be released and not stick to the cell.

Neuraminidase inhibitors such as oseltamivir and zanamivir block release of progeny virions.

Example: H1N1 and H3N2 are subtypes named for their H and N proteins.
cards.searchQuery: hemagglutinin neuraminidase function oseltamivir influenza

cards.title: In a plaque assay for bacteriophage, in what unit is the infectious titer reported?
cards.body:
Plaque-forming units (PFU) per mL.

Each clear zone (plaque) in a bacterial lawn arises from a single infectious phage, which lysed the surrounding cells.

Example: 25 plaques from $0.1\,\mathrm{mL}$ of a $10^{-6}$ dilution gives $25 \times 10 \times 10^{6} = 2.5 \times 10^{8}$ PFU/mL.
cards.searchQuery: plaque assay PFU phage titer calculation

cards.title: What infectious agent consists only of misfolded protein, with no nucleic acid, and causes Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease and bovine spongiform encephalopathy?
cards.body:
A prion.

The abnormal $\beta$-sheet-rich form, PrP$^{\mathrm{Sc}}$, converts normal host PrP$^{\mathrm{C}}$ into more of itself. Prions resist heat, radiation and ordinary sterilization.

Watch out: prion diseases are fatal neurodegenerative disorders, not infections that antibiotics or antivirals can treat.
cards.searchQuery: prion misfolded protein Creutzfeldt-Jakob bovine spongiform encephalopathy

cards.title: What is a viroid, and which hosts does it infect?
cards.body:
A viroid is a short, circular, naked **RNA** with no capsid, and it infects **plants**.

It does not code for any protein. It relies on host enzymes for replication and can stunt or kill crops.

Key idea: viroid = RNA only; prion = protein only; virus = nucleic acid plus protein coat.
cards.searchQuery: viroid circular RNA plant pathogen no capsid

cards.title: Where does herpes simplex virus 1 (HSV-1) remain latent, and where does varicella-zoster virus (VZV) stay latent after chickenpox?
cards.body:
HSV-1 lies latent in the **trigeminal ganglia**; VZV lies latent in **dorsal root ganglia** (and cranial nerve ganglia).

Reactivation causes cold sores (HSV-1) and **shingles** (VZV) along the dermatome served by the nerve.

Example: shingles appears as a painful unilateral band of vesicles.
cards.searchQuery: herpes simplex latency trigeminal ganglia varicella zoster shingles

cards.title: How does acyclovir selectively target herpesvirus-infected cells?
cards.body:
It is a **guanosine analog** that is phosphorylated first by the viral thymidine kinase, so it is activated only in infected cells.

The triphosphate form then inhibits viral DNA polymerase and terminates the growing chain.

Example: acyclovir treats HSV and VZV; resistance arises from loss of viral thymidine kinase.
cards.searchQuery: acyclovir mechanism viral thymidine kinase DNA polymerase

cards.title: Which DNA virus, especially types 16 and 18, causes most cervical cancers?
cards.body:
Human papillomavirus (HPV).

The viral proteins E6 and E7 inactivate the host tumor suppressors p53 and Rb. A vaccine against the high-risk types prevents infection, and Pap smears and HPV tests screen for disease.

Key idea: HPV also causes common warts and some oropharyngeal cancers.
cards.searchQuery: human papillomavirus HPV 16 18 cervical cancer E6 E7

cards.title: Which sterol is found in fungal cell membranes, in place of the cholesterol of animal cells, and is the target of amphotericin B and the azole drugs?
cards.body:
Ergosterol.

Amphotericin B binds ergosterol and forms pores. Azoles (such as fluconazole) block its synthesis. Because human cells use cholesterol, this gives some selective toxicity.

Watch out: amphotericin B can still harm human cells at high doses, notably the kidneys.
cards.searchQuery: ergosterol fungal membrane amphotericin B azoles

cards.title: Which polysaccharide, a polymer of N-acetylglucosamine, is the main structural component of fungal cell walls?
cards.body:
Chitin.

It is also the material of arthropod exoskeletons. Fungal walls contain chitin and glucans, not peptidoglycan, which is why antibacterial drugs like penicillin do not affect fungi.
cards.searchQuery: fungal cell wall chitin glucan

cards.title: What does it mean for a pathogenic fungus to be thermally dimorphic?
cards.body:
It grows as a **mold** in the environment (about $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$) and as a **yeast** in the host (about $37\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$).

Molds form branching hyphae. Yeasts are single cells that reproduce by budding.

Example: $\textit{Histoplasma capsulatum}$ is a mold in soil and a yeast in human macrophages.
cards.searchQuery: thermally dimorphic fungi mold yeast Histoplasma

cards.title: Which yeast, part of the normal flora of the mouth, gut and vagina, causes thrush and vulvovaginal infections when the flora is disturbed?
cards.body:
$\textit{Candida albicans}$.

Predisposing factors include antibiotic use, diabetes and immunosuppression. Thrush appears as white plaques on the oral mucosa.

Example: in the lab, $\textit{C. albicans}$ forms germ tubes at $37\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ in serum.
cards.searchQuery: Candida albicans thrush normal flora yeast

cards.title: Which protozoan genus causes malaria, and which mosquito transmits it to humans?
cards.body:
$\textit{Plasmodium}$, transmitted by the female $\textit{Anopheles}$ mosquito.

Parasites multiply in liver cells and then in red blood cells. Rupture of red cells causes cyclic fevers. $\textit{Plasmodium falciparum}$ is the most dangerous species.

Key idea: sickle-cell trait gives some protection against severe falciparum malaria.
cards.searchQuery: Plasmodium malaria Anopheles mosquito life cycle

cards.title: Which flagellated protozoan, acquired from cysts in contaminated water, causes foul-smelling, fatty diarrhea in hikers?
cards.body:
$\textit{Giardia lamblia}$.

Also called $\textit{G. intestinalis}$. Cysts survive chlorination, so filtering or boiling water is needed. Trophozoites attach to the small intestine and impair absorption.

Tip: Giardia is treated with metronidazole.
cards.searchQuery: Giardia lamblia cysts diarrhea water metronidazole

cards.title: Which protozoan, whose definitive host is the cat, can cross the placenta and harm a fetus if the mother is first infected during pregnancy?
cards.body:
$\textit{Toxoplasma gondii}$.

People are infected from cat feces (oocysts) or undercooked meat with tissue cysts. Congenital infection can cause hydrocephalus and chorioretinitis.

Tip: pregnant women should avoid cleaning cat litter.
cards.searchQuery: Toxoplasma gondii cat pregnancy congenital

cards.title: At $15\,\mathrm{psi}$ of steam pressure, an autoclave reaches what temperature in $^\circ\mathrm{C}$? Give the number only.
cards.body:
121

The typical cycle is $121\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ at $15\,\mathrm{psi}$ for at least 15 minutes. Moist heat kills by denaturing proteins and destroys endospores.

Why: pressurized steam raises the temperature above $100\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, so it kills much faster than boiling water.
cards.searchQuery: autoclave 121 C 15 psi sterilization time

cards.title: Spores of which organism are used as the biological indicator to confirm that an autoclave is sterilizing properly?
cards.body:
$\textit{Geobacillus stearothermophilus}$ (formerly $\textit{Bacillus stearothermophilus}$).

Its spores are very heat resistant. If they are killed, the cycle should also have killed all common contaminants.

Watch out: chemical indicator tape only shows that a temperature was reached, not that sterilization occurred.
cards.searchQuery: Geobacillus stearothermophilus spores autoclave biological indicator

cards.title: What is the difference between a disinfectant and an antiseptic, and how do both differ from sterilization?
cards.body:
A **disinfectant** is used on inanimate objects; an **antiseptic** is safe for living tissue. **Sterilization** destroys all microbial life, including spores.

Both disinfection and antisepsis reduce pathogens but need not kill endospores.

Example: bleach disinfects a countertop; povidone-iodine is an antiseptic for skin before surgery.
cards.searchQuery: disinfectant versus antiseptic versus sterilization difference

cards.title: What is the difference between a bacteriostatic and a bactericidal agent?
cards.body:
A **bacteriostatic** agent **inhibits growth** while the drug is present; a **bactericidal** agent **kills** the bacteria.

Bacteriostatic drugs rely on the immune system to clear the bacteria, and growth resumes if the drug is removed.

Example: tetracyclines are generally bacteriostatic; penicillins are bactericidal.
cards.searchQuery: bacteriostatic versus bactericidal definition examples

cards.title: Why is 70% ethanol a better disinfectant than 95% ethanol?
cards.body:
Water is needed for protein denaturation. At 95%, the cell surface proteins coagulate quickly and seal the cell, which **blocks entry** of more alcohol.

70% penetrates better and kills more reliably.

Watch out: alcohols do not kill endospores, and they evaporate quickly.
cards.searchQuery: 70 percent ethanol better than 95 percent disinfectant protein denaturation

cards.title: What pore size in micrometers is commonly used for membrane filters that remove bacteria and so sterilize heat-sensitive liquids? Give the number only.
cards.body:
0.22

Filters with $0.22\,\mu\mathrm{m}$ pores trap bacteria but not viruses, which are far smaller. They are used for media with heat-labile vitamins or antibiotics, and for IV solutions.

Watch out: filtration removes bacteria physically, so it does not inactivate viruses or toxins.
cards.searchQuery: 0.22 micrometer membrane filter sterilization bacteria

cards.title: What is selective toxicity, and why does it make many antibiotics safe for humans?
cards.body:
A drug harms the **microbe** much more than the **host**, because it hits a structure or pathway that is absent in human cells.

Examples: peptidoglycan synthesis (penicillin), 70S ribosomes (tetracycline, macrolides) and bacterial folate synthesis (sulfonamides).

Watch out: it is not absolute. Aminoglycosides can still damage human kidneys and ears.
cards.searchQuery: selective toxicity antibiotics bacterial targets

cards.title: How do penicillins and other $\beta$-lactams kill bacteria?
cards.body:
They bind **penicillin-binding proteins** (PBPs) and block the **transpeptidation** step that cross-links peptidoglycan chains.

Growing cells keep making autolysins but cannot build a strong wall, so they burst from osmotic pressure.

Key idea: they kill only actively growing cells, and they are generally bactericidal.
cards.searchQuery: penicillin mechanism penicillin-binding proteins transpeptidase

cards.title: Which enzyme, made by many resistant bacteria, hydrolyzes the $\beta$-lactam ring and inactivates penicillins?
cards.body:
$\beta$-lactamase (penicillinase).

To get around it, amoxicillin is combined with the inhibitor **clavulanic acid**, which binds and inactivates the enzyme.

Example: amoxicillin-clavulanate is a common treatment for $\beta$-lactamase-producing strains.
cards.searchQuery: beta-lactamase penicillinase resistance clavulanic acid

cards.title: What is the mechanism of methicillin resistance in MRSA?
cards.body:
The **mecA** gene encodes an altered penicillin-binding protein, **PBP2a**, that has very low affinity for nearly all $\beta$-lactams.

Wall synthesis continues even in the presence of the drug. Treatment of serious MRSA infections often uses vancomycin.

Watch out: MRSA resistance is not due to $\beta$-lactamase; it is due to an altered target.
cards.searchQuery: MRSA mecA PBP2a methicillin resistance mechanism

cards.title: Which antibiotic classes bind the 30S ribosomal subunit and which bind the 50S subunit?
cards.body:
**30S**: aminoglycosides and tetracyclines. **50S**: macrolides, chloramphenicol, clindamycin and linezolid.

Bacterial ribosomes are 70S (30S plus 50S), unlike the 80S ribosomes of the human cytoplasm.

Mnemonic: "buy AT 30, CCEL at 50": Aminoglycosides, Tetracyclines at 30; Chloramphenicol, Clindamycin, Erythromycin (macrolides), Linezolid at 50.
cards.searchQuery: antibiotics 30S 50S ribosome aminoglycosides tetracycline macrolides

cards.title: Which bacterial enzyme, a type II topoisomerase that introduces negative supercoils into DNA, is the main target of fluoroquinolones such as ciprofloxacin?
cards.body:
DNA gyrase.

Fluoroquinolones also inhibit topoisomerase IV. Blocking these enzymes prevents DNA replication and causes lethal DNA breaks.

Example: gyrase is the main target in Gram-negative bacteria, and topoisomerase IV in many Gram-positives.
cards.searchQuery: fluoroquinolone ciprofloxacin DNA gyrase topoisomerase IV

cards.title: Why is the combination of a sulfonamide and trimethoprim synergistic against bacteria?
cards.body:
They block **two sequential steps** in folate synthesis. Sulfonamides are PABA analogs that inhibit **dihydropteroate synthase**; trimethoprim inhibits **dihydrofolate reductase**.

Humans do not make folate; they obtain it from the diet, so the drugs are selective.

Example: trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is commonly used for urinary tract infections.
cards.searchQuery: sulfonamide trimethoprim sequential blockade folate synthesis

cards.title: What does the abbreviation MIC stand for in antimicrobial susceptibility testing?
cards.body:
Minimum inhibitory concentration.

It is the **lowest concentration** of an antimicrobial that prevents visible growth of a bacterium in broth or agar after overnight incubation.

Watch out: MIC does not by itself say whether a drug is bactericidal.
cards.searchQuery: minimum inhibitory concentration MIC antimicrobial susceptibility

cards.title: Name four general mechanisms by which bacteria become resistant to antibiotics.
cards.body:
1. **Enzymatic inactivation** of the drug ($\beta$-lactamases)
2. **Altered target** (PBP2a in MRSA)
3. **Efflux pumps** that export the drug
4. **Reduced permeability** (fewer or altered porins)

Resistance genes spread by plasmids, transposons and horizontal transfer.

Why: selective pressure from antibiotic use enriches resistant cells, so misuse speeds resistance.
cards.searchQuery: antibiotic resistance mechanisms efflux enzymatic inactivation altered target
